Question: A positive integer \(n\) is “nice” if there is a positive integer \(m\) with exactly four positive divisors (including \(1\) and \(m\)) such that the sum of the four divisors is equal to \(n.\) How many numbers in the set \[\{ 2010,2011,2012,\dotsc,2019 \}\] are nice?
Solution:
Having exactly four divisors severely restricts \(m\). If it has only one prime factor, then \(m=p^k\) has divisors \(1,p,\ldots,p^k\), so \(k=3\). If it has two distinct prime factors \(p,q\), then \(1,p,q,pq\) are already four divisors. Thus \(m\) must equal \(pq\), since otherwise \(m\) itself would be a fifth divisor. These observations cover every possibility.

For \(m=p^3\), the divisor sum is
\[
1+p+p^2+p^3.
\]
This expression increases with the positive integer \(p\). Its values at \(12\) and \(13\) are \(1885\) and \(2380\), respectively. Therefore it cannot lie between \(2010\) and \(2019\).

For \(m=pq\), where \(p\ne q\) are primes, the divisor sum is
\[
1+p+q+pq=(p+1)(q+1).
\]
If one prime is \(2\), the other is odd, so this sum is divisible by \(6\). If both primes are odd, the sum is divisible by \(4\). In the specified interval, the only candidates are consequently
\[
2010,\quad2012,\quad2016.
\]

For \(2010\), divisibility by \(4\) fails, so one prime would have to be \(2\). Then \(3(q+1)=2010\), giving \(q=669=3\cdot223\), which is not prime.

For \(2012\), divisibility by \(6\) fails, so both primes would have to be odd. Dividing their two even factors by \(2\) would give
\[
\frac{p+1}{2}\cdot\frac{q+1}{2}=503.
\]
Both factors are at least \(2\), which is impossible because \(503\) is prime. To check this primality, its square root is less than \(23\); it is not divisible by \(2,3,5\), and division by \(7,11,13,17,19\) gives remainders \(6,8,9,10,9\), respectively.

Finally,
\[
2016=(3+1)(503+1).
\]
Thus \(m=3\cdot503=1509\) has exactly the four divisors \(1,3,503,1509\), whose sum is \(2016\).

Only \(2016\) is nice, so the answer is \(\boxed{1}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
